newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Birch noncommittal on compulsory pension plan.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Birch noncommittal on compulsory pension plan.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch on Tuesday said he still favoured a voluntary retirement savings scheme over a compulsory scheme.

Asked if he would vote yes or no in a September referendum on the government's proposed compulsory Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS), unveiled on Monday, Birch declined to make a definite statement of support.
"My instincts are with a voluntary scheme but the choice is with the voters," Birch said.
He added that he was pleased with the design of the compulsory scheme to be put to public vote.
"I think it is an excellent scheme. If the voters say yes, they can do so with confidence that the scheme is well constructed."
A government white paper published on Monday said the pension scheme would require all earners who can to save about NZ$120,000 (US$81,000) toward the cost of their pension.

The scheme would initially require workers to contribute three percent of their income to the scheme. On retirement, the savings would be used to buy an annuity to deliver income equivalent to the current state pension.
The contribution level would rise to eight percent of income over five years, provided the government can afford the tax cuts it has promised in order to offset the higher contributions.
Compensatory tax cuts are guaranteed in the first year, but thereafter would only happen "when fiscally sustainable".
The compulsory pension scheme, to be implemented in July next year if passed in the referendum, was a key part of the election campaign of Treasurer Winston Peters' party, New Zealand First.
NZ First is the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative National Party.
A recent poll of 933 people by financial services group Colonial showed opposition to the scheme had risen to 63 percent from 59 percent in May.
